summary: The assessee assessee was a Hindu undivided family and was assessed to income tax under the Income tax Act, 1922. The Income tax Officer assessed the income of the assessee on the basis of the valuation of the assets. The Income Tax Officer held that the assets were not liable to income tax. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Appellate Assistant Commissioner. The Appellate Tribunal held that the assessee was not liable to tax under the Act. The High Court held that the valuation of assets was not liable for income tax. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the assessee that the valuation was not liable under the Act because the valuation was made in the course of inter se business and that the valuation made in the books of account was not liable in the sense of the expression "any asset" in section 2(1) of the Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Courts have held that the value of assets was liable to tax. The High court was right in holding that the valuation in the books was not liable. [703E] 2. The High 's view that the valuation should be made in the manner prescribed by the statute is correct. [704E] 3. The HighCourt was right in taking the view that the value in the books should be determined in the manner provided by the statute. [705E] 4. The High Powered by the High Court in the case of Commissioner of Income tax vs M/s. T.N. & Co., [1963] Supp. 2 S.C.R. 869, referred to.

The assessee was a Hindu undivided family and was a Hindu joint family. The Income tax Officer assessed the income of the assessee to tax under section 10(1) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the assessee was not a Hindu undivided and that the Income tax Officer was not competent to assess the income of that family. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The income of a family is income from the business of a Hindu joint Hindu family. The income of the family is income of the Hindu undivided family. The assessee is not a Hindu joint and Hindu undivided family, and the income of such family is income. The income is income of that person. The workmen in the present case were workmen of the appellant company. The workmen were paid wages for the period of their employment. The workmen had not been paid wages in the same manner as the workmen were paid in respect thereof, and that they had been paid in respect whereof the workmen were given wages for the work. The appellant was the tenant of a flat in Bombay. The appellant was the owner of the flat. The appellant had been in possession of the flat and the flat was in the possession of the appellant. The appellant must be held to have been in possession and possession of that property. The appellant did not have any right to continue his flat. The right to continue it was a right of the appellant to continue the premises. The appellant cannot be convicted under sections 7(1) and 7 of the Bombay Rent Act. The right of the respondent to continue the building was a right which was not a right of a landlord. The right was not a mere right of a tenant to continue the same. The right cannot be determined by the trial court. The right can be determined by a court of law. The right must be determined by an agreement of lease. The right may be determined by agreement of lease and the right to continue a building is a right to remain in possession. The right has to be determined by contract of lease. It is not necessary that the right must be exercised in the same manner as the right to remain with the tenant. The right conferred by section 7(2) is a right which is a right conferred by the statute. The right under section 7 is a right in the same way as the right conferred by it. The right which is conferred by the Act is a right not conferred by the law. The question is whether the right conferred under section 7 can be determined in the same terms as the right of a person to continue the business of the tenant. It is well settled that the right to terminate the tenancy is a right and not a right which can be determined under the statute. It is also well settled that a right conferred under the statute is a right. The right in the present case is a right created by the statute and the right conferred on the tenant is a right under the statute and it is not necessary to determine whether the right of the tenant is in the nature of a right or not. The right created by section 7 is not a right created under the statute but a right created in the nature. The right given to the tenant under section 7 (1) is a statutory right. The appellant has a right to terminate his tenancy under section 7. The right, therefore, is a right, and the right of an owner to continue the tenancy is not a statutory right and is not a mere statutory right.

The High Court held that the suit had been barred by limitation and that the suit could not be dismissed on the ground of limitation. The High court held that the appellant was not a tenant within the meaning of section 2(f) of the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1948. The High Judge held that the Act was not applicable to the suit and that the Act had not been applied to the suit. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the Act did not apply to the suit as it was not applicable in the case of a tenant who had been evicted from the land in the West Bengal. HELD : (i) The Act was not a law which was not applicable for the purpose of the Act. The Act was a law which had been passed in the case in which the Act was passed. The Act did not have the effect of extending the period of limitation for the purpose. The Act had not come into force in the case. The Act could not be applied to the proceedings in the case where the Act had come into force. The Act, therefore, was not applicable. [619 D] (ii) The Act had no application to the proceedings before the Court in which the suit was filed. The Act does not apply to proceedings in the Court in the case which had been instituted before the commencement of the Act and the Act had no retrospective operation. The Act is a law which has been passed in respect of the land which had been allotted to the tenant. [620 D] (iii) The Act does have the effect that the Act has not been applied in the case when the Act had been passed. The provisions of the Act are not applicable to proceedings in which the proceedings were instituted before the date of the commencement of Act. [621 D] (iv) The Act is not applicable to a proceeding in which the proceeding was instituted before the coming into force of the Act, but is a law relating to the subject matter of the suit. [622 D] (v) The Act has no retrospective operation and the Act has no application to proceedings in a case where the proceeding was initiated before the commencement. [623 D] (vi) The Act cannot be applied to proceedings in respect of which the proceeding had been instituted after the commencement of this Act.
